Just a couple of months or so after a Times piece broke the news that Letterboxd — a social media network where ~30 million users log and review movies they’ve watched — had been attracting takeover interest from a host of names in the entertainment industry, it seems that the Grey Lady herself is now leading the charge. Last week, the NYT reported that its parent company had entered into advanced talks to buy the platform for around $330 million. Letterboxd reps and The New York Times Company chose to take non-speaking roles in the report, though sources close to the discussions were on hand to add color. Apparently, Sony Pictures and ever-popular artsy production house A24 had both been circling the platform, with the latter dropping out as the potential takeover bids rose. For its part in the now exclusive negotiations, the Times Company has reportedly discussed keeping Matthew Buchanan and Karl von Randow at the helm, the pair having launched Letterboxd together at a Brooklyn web conference in 2011 . At the time, the final installment in the Harry Potter movie franchise was topping the box office. The media landscape has changed a bit since. For instance, never has the artist’s eternal “everyone’s a critic” complaint been truer, as platforms like Letterboxd and the Amazon -owned Goodreads have almost gamified art consumption; films are something to log, books are something to shelve. Just looking at Letterboxd’s analytics gives you a decent picture of how the business of letting cinephiles record and review their latest watches has boomed in recent years. Given how user figures have ballooned since the pandemic era, with each metric in Letterboxd’s annual year-end review rising at least four times from 2020 to 2025, it’s little wonder that some within the industry have started to refer to younger fervent film fans as the “ Letterboxd Generation .” The rising popularity of platform features such as “ Four Favorites ,” now a mainstay question for celebs stopped on red carpets and stuck in press junkets, as well as getting one of the biggest names in media onboard, makes it hard to imagine a world where Letterboxd users aren’t logging 1 billion+ movies on the platform each year at some point in the near future. As The New York Times Company’s metamorphosis from a news peddler to games-entertainment-product reviews-and-recipes behemoth that runs a side gig sending reporters to war zones continues, deals like this only make more sense. In fairness, the company behind America’s paper of record has provided much more than the news for a while now, having long realized that it needs more than straight reporting to keep modern audiences engaged (and paying up) in the digital age. Indeed, just like Letterboxd hopes that the financial backing and increased visibility from any potential sale will help juice their user numbers and boost its revenue, the Times likely views the Letterboxd deal — like the acquisitions of Wordle and The Athletic before it — as another potential stepping stone towards its goal to 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027. 🏈 NFL: It’s an NFC East showdown tonight between the Washington Commanders and the New York Giants, with New York a 57% favorite . body_text: As companies like DoorDash , Uber and Amazon race to deliver packages and burritos via drones, an unlikely competitor is giving them a run for their money: a chimpanzee sanctuary in Florida . After heavy rains flooded the sanctuary's roads, staff turned to a drone to deliver food to Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee stranded by the rising waters. His order? A paper bag full of bananas, with some blankets thrown in. Kaleb enjoyed his airborne meal before eventually making his way across the water on a rope. No word on whether he tipped. Hims’ margins, not unlike many of its customers, are getting slimmer. Can peptides help it get back to profit growth? Both Eli Lilly and Novo (formerly known as Novo Nordisk ) reported sales numbers that beat estimates and hiked their outlooks. Earlier this year, both companies released oral GLP-1s that have by all accounts been flying off the pharmacy shelves without cannibalizing sales from its legacy injectable products. Over the years, Lilly and Novo have increasingly sold the drugs through direct-to-consumer channels, often through partnerships with telehealth companies like Hims & Hers. Hims used to sell knock-off versions of Novo’s injectable drugs, which were produced in compounding pharmacies (some owned by Hims, others through partnerships) and officially marketed as bespoke treatments. After more than a year of threats and a brief legal battle with Novo, Hims no longer sells those high-margin knock-offs. Now, it offers Novo and Lilly’s branded drugs on its platforms, which carry significantly lower margins. The company’s profits have taken a hit as a result. On Monday it reported a surprise loss for the quarter along with sales and subscriber count numbers that missed expectations. It also cut its outlook for the year. “We had, as you all saw in the last quarter or two, just a massive transformation of the business, moving from the compounding offerings to the partnership with Novo,” Hims CEO Andrew Dudum told analysts on Monday. Hims also said it will begin offering some unapproved peptide treatments this month after US regulators eased restrictions. Dudum said the new offering will include glutathione, NAD, sermorelin and B12, with BPC-157 and TB-500 potentially coming later, subject to regulatory approval. For the unacquainted, peptides are under-studied supplements , usually injectable, that have grown in popularity in recent years because of their purported health benefits. As of now, consumers are bypassing the FDA by buying vials of peptides labeled “for research use only” and then conducting that research on themselves. Importantly for Hims: the company can sell these treatments while controlling much of the supply chain, from manufacturing to distribution. While it’s unclear how big the market truly is, peptides could offer the kind of attractive margins Hims enjoyed when it was selling compounded GLP-1s. Hims has already acquired a peptide manufacturing facility in Menlo Park, California, and says it's seen a “tremendous amount of excitement” from customers on its waitlist, per Dudum. But the company isn't expecting the new business to contribute meaningfully to revenue in the current quarter. Hims does best when it behaves like a drugmaker , selling its own products versus made in an industrial pharmacy rather than serving as the sleek, neutral colored liaison between you and an actual pharmaceutical company. Selling compounded GLP-1s was very lucrative for Hims. Peptides could give it another shot at that business model. But the company is once again betting on a category where the regulatory ground is still shifting beneath its feet. “In healthcare, whoever owns the customer relationship wins,” Dudum said. title: 👀 Affair valuation
body_text: The American consumer is exhausted and enraged by rising prices, and ready, according to consumer data, to spend a $1 billion on packaged food that’s labeled “seed-oil free.” Seed oils are, of course, the fashionable, if scientifically dubious, boogeyman. Data doesn’t back up claims of various health harms caused by seed oils but the Americans aren’t letting that get in the way: seed-oil-free products saw a 72% gain compared to a year earlier, and sales of seed-oil-free salty snacks climbed 87%, compared to just 2.9% for products without the label, Bloomberg News reported based on NIQ data. Big food companies like PepsiCo and ConAgra are making the switch by relying on olive and avocado oil. Markets bounced back Monday, rising after last week’s AI-trade induced wipeout, despite news over the weekend about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy (more on that story below.) “We’ve spent all this time worrying about AI cybersecurity risks when our true vulnerabilities come from human frailty,” was how Entrypoint’s Luke Kawa summed it up . On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang released a statement admitting to an extra-marital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang’s statement comes after the New York Times first reported on the CEO’s “close” relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. American officials, the NYT reported, had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset and involved in helping China evade constraints limiting its ability to import high-powered AI chips. Nvidia’s board of directors has opened an investigation into Huang’s conduct but has said it does not believe US national security or its own intellectual property have been compromised. The specifics don’t look good: Alice Huang is the CEO of Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that has been an absolutely massive buyer of Nvidia chips. She is believed by US intelligence officials to have been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Financial Times reported . The MSS fulfills a role similar to a combination of the CIA, FBI, and NSA. The US Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it was buying Nvidia AI chips in order to smuggle them into China before the probe was suddenly called off and transferred to the Justice Department late last year, the New York Times reported Monday . That switch came after Nvidia’s general counsel emailed Commerce Department investigators seeking information about the inquiry. Other tech stocks surged on Monday – the PHLX Semiconductor index gained almost 7% despite Nvdia falling about 4.5% on the day. As Kawa pointed out in yesterday’s Entrypoint newsletter, the market has for months now been a bit skeptical about the medium-term outlook for Nvdia’s profits. If you assume the chip giant’s quarter-on-quarter earnings-per-share growth dips to less than half its current average and investors give the stock a valuation in its recent lowest quartile, Kawa ballparks that Nvidia would be worth… about what it is today. Score one for the strong-form efficient markets hypothesis , I guess. At the same time, it’s hard exactly to know how Jensen Huang will respond to being put under a very new kind of public spotlight, and whether investors will have confidence in anyone but him to deliver the kind of returns he has overseen.
